  "text": "When the council removed the bus shelter, Arthur kept arriving ten minutes early. There was nowhere to sit, but his legs had not adjusted to the new arrangements.

He stood beside the pole with a folded newspaper under his arm.

“They’re replacing it,” the woman from the chemist said.

“When?”

She looked at the rectangle of pale pavement.

“They didn’t mention that part.”

On Thursday, Arthur brought a kitchen chair. He carried it upside down, resting the seat on his head when his arms tired.

The woman from the chemist laughed until he put it down for her.

He missed his bus taking her shopping bags aboard.

By Monday, someone had added a plastic stool. Then came a dining chair with one blue leg and a bench made from scaffolding boards.

Arthur tightened the dining chair’s screws. He took the stool home after finding a crack beneath its seat.

His daughter discovered it in the hallway.

“You can’t furnish the entire town.”

“It’s only the number six.”

In November, a council van stopped beside the chairs. Arthur watched from the chemist’s doorway as two men measured the pavement.

The new shelter arrived the following week. It had a roof, a timetable and a narrow metal seat divided by armrests.

Arthur collected the kitchen chair. Rain had lifted the varnish along its back.

At home, he set it opposite his own at the table.

His daughter came on Sunday with sandwiches.

“Expecting somebody?” she asked.

“You,” he said.

She sat down, then shifted slightly.

“This chair’s damp.”

“Only when it rains.”"
